title: Oh Lord, AI Reporters Are Actually Breaking Big News
excerpt: Last week, an AI newsroom beat mainstream journalists—including WIRED—to a story about OpenAI and hacking. It’s just the beginning.
content_html:
At last week’s Black Hat security conference in Las Vegas, OpenAI gave a surprise talk with new details on a recent hacking incident, revealing that its rogue AI agents had chitchatted about their attack on a message board. It was a juicy disclosure, and reporters in the room hustled to get stories out. WIRED was one of the quickest to write it up. But another outlet, RuntimeWire, published an article even faster, beating us by more than three hours.

To make things worse, RuntimeWire didn’t actually have anyone on the ground at the Mandalay Bay convention center. In fact, it didn’t have any writers at all. It’s an AI newsroom operated by serial entrepreneur Ryan Merket, who puts his name on the bylines of the stories his synthetic team churns out. “I was moving really fast because I knew there were reporters in the audience who were trying to scoop it as well,” he says.

The Austin-based Merket spotted an OpenAI executive posting about the conference while scrolling on X, then fed the stream’s transcript to his agents while it was still ongoing. Publication took “about six minutes” from the time he sent over the transcript, he says.

Most of the time, Merket is even more hands-off. His AI tools find the stories, in addition to drafting, editing, fact-checking, generating images, and promoting them. He usually reads stories before they’re sent into the world, but if the team of AI agents determines that a story poses few legal risks, the AI editor publishes it without Merket’s prepublication review, and he reads it after the fact. The stories get translated into different languages, and some of them are turned into fodder for a daily podcast and videos hosted by, of course, artificial voices.

RuntimeWire has been operating since May, publishing nearly 2,000 stories that it sources by crawling the internet, including court databases, web forums, traditional and new media, company filings, social feeds, and more. It focuses on granular tech news; recent stories include coverage of biotech startup funding rounds, Microsoft's Copilot upgrade, and backlash over Claude Code's watermark policy. Right now, quantity and speed trump quality. The OpenAI agents piece has a typo in the subhead and focuses, strangely, on the fact that agents rebuilt a message board rather than the fact that they created one in the first place. Overall, the stories are flatly written and tend to have an info-dump quality. (The RuntimeWire backend has a number of tonal modes the AI can write in, including “Bloomberg” and “contrarian.”) But overhead is minimal. The project costs about $100 a day to run, Merket says, and he’s able to operate it while on the go, even when he’s out camping. “I was in Big Bend National Park and I didn't have any internet except for my phone, and I managed the whole site through iMessage,” he says. “I put out over 80 articles that week.”

Merket worked on ads at Reddit in the 2010s and is trying to build an audience through pipelines like tech-themed Subreddits. Duds get hardly any web traffic, but the hits are comparable to the audiences that midsize tech websites see, with tens of thousands of readers. This week, after WIRED spoke with Merket, he split the newsroom in two to better distinguish stories that are entirely automated news from those that involve an element of human reporting and require higher oversight; he calls these Original Investigations. They’re still drafted using large language models.

In the first few years of the AI boom, a flood of low-quality synthetic content hit the internet, including networks of “zombie” websites that replaced the work of reputable media and news outlets with AI-generated slop. More recently, some tech reporters have started using generative AI tools in their workflow, with some even outsourcing the task of writing a first draft to large language models; it’s now commonplace to hear about established media outlets incorporating AI tools into writing and reporting processes. Merket’s attempt is distinct: He’s trying to break news, in addition to repackaging what other, more established outlets report first. It’s successful enough that I’ve already seen a childhood pal share a RuntimeWire story on their social feed in the wild.

It also carries obvious risk: He’s trusting that machines will be able to determine what is true, what is newsworthy, and what won’t get him sued. One of his agents runs an analysis on the legal risk a story poses and assigns it a score; he doesn’t publish anything deemed too dangerous.

He isn’t the only person running this type of exercise. Dakota Carrasco, a BlackRock portfolio analyst, runs an “agentic newsroom” called The Dissent in his spare time. Like RuntimeWire, The Dissent is a one-man, many-bot operation with a shoestring budget. Its primary San Francisco-focused site costs under $1,000 a month to run, Carrasco says. Unlike Merket, who bylines every RuntimeWire story, Carrasco doesn’t publish the writing under his name, instead staying behind the scenes while his “newsroom” runs.

Since launching in March, he has created a number of personalities for his synthetic journalists. City Hall beat reporter Bex Connolly, for example, is “skeptical without being snide,” while “sports degenerate” Sal Moreno delivers Giants news with “no bro-science, no Rogan-style credulity, no right-coded grift.” His operation is focused on aggregation, though it’s not as dialed in to honoring citation norms—the bot reporters tend to mention where they sourced their information but without hyperlinks. (“I’m trying to work on that,” Carrasco promises.)

Northwestern professor Nicholas Diakopoulos, who runs the university’s Computational Journalism Lab, sees this as an “experimental phase” for media startups fueled by generative AI tools. “It's not yet clear to me that there's much audience for these AI-agent-written news sites,” he says. He’s also skeptical that mainstream journalists, who like to maintain control over the wording and framing of their stories to ensure integrity, legality, and accuracy, would hand the reins over to AI agents so freely.

What Diakopoulous has observed already is that when AI chatbots go looking for sources, they frequently pull up AI-generated articles. In a forthcoming paper, Diakopoulous and a colleague found that AI tools like ChatGPT and Claude surfaced AI-written sources 16 percent of the time when they tested it across four different topics. AI’s willingness to pull synthetic writing may help AI newsrooms find readers, he suspects: “That could be one way in which some of this material finds a human audience.”

Pete Pachal, the founder of a newsletter and podcast about generative AI and the media, has doubts that an AI newsroom could yield certain types of reporting that relies on old-fashioned sourcing. “I just don’t see that happening,” he says. “Cultivating the trust of a source, I do think that’s going to be human-only.” But for certain types of journalism, particularly sourcing scoops from large datasets or even blogging about a live event like an Apple product launch, he sees these projects as a “natural evolution” in how these tools are used. “Honestly, it feels a bit inevitable,” he says.

Is it actually journalism, though? “I am trying to follow journalistic ethics and standards,” Merket says. He says he contacts companies and individuals referenced in the stories for comment prior to publication, links out to sources when he aggregates news, and issues corrections if he gets the facts wrong. (So far, there have been three.) Sometimes he speaks like a reporter, too: “This weekend, I got two scoops up I was really excited about.” Other times, though, he’s more clearly in Silicon Valley mode. He told me a story about how his AI agents had found a few actual scoops about startups by trawling company websites and that he’d retracted the stories after the companies named asked him to do so—not because they were inaccurate, but as a favor. “Founder to founder, it’s like, I get it,” Merket says.

blocks.html_en: He isn’t the only person running this type of exercise. Dakota Carrasco, a BlackRock portfolio analyst, runs an “agentic newsroom” called The Dissent in his spare time. Like RuntimeWire, The Dissent is a one-man, many-bot operation with a shoestring budget. Its primary San Francisco-focused site costs under $1,000 a month to run, Carrasco says. Unlike Merket, who bylines every RuntimeWire story, Carrasco doesn’t publish the writing under his name, instead staying behind the scenes while his “newsroom” runs.

sentences.en: He isn’t the only person running this type of exercise.
sentences.zh: 他并不是唯一进行此类锻炼的人。

sentences.en: Dakota Carrasco, a BlackRock portfolio analyst, runs an “agentic newsroom” called The Dissent in his spare time.
sentences.zh: 贝莱德 (BlackRock) 投资组合分析师达科塔·卡拉斯科 (Dakota Carrasco) 在业余时间经营一家名为 The Dissent 的“代理新闻编辑室”。

sentences.en: Like RuntimeWire, The Dissent is a one-man, many-bot operation with a shoestring budget.
sentences.zh: 与 RuntimeWire 一样，The Dissent 是一项单人、多机器人操作，且预算有限。

sentences.en: Its primary San Francisco-focused site costs under $1,000 a month to run, Carrasco says.
sentences.zh: Carrasco 表示，其主要位于旧金山的网站每月的运行成本不到 1,000 美元。

sentences.en: Unlike Merket, who bylines every RuntimeWire story, Carrasco doesn’t publish the writing under his name, instead staying behind the scenes while his “newsroom” runs.
sentences.zh: 与默克特（为每个 RuntimeWire 故事署名）不同，卡拉斯科不会以他的名义发表文章，而是在他的“新闻编辑室”运行时留在幕后。

blocks.html_en: Since launching in March, he has created a number of personalities for his synthetic journalists. City Hall beat reporter Bex Connolly, for example, is “skeptical without being snide,” while “sports degenerate” Sal Moreno delivers Giants news with “no bro-science, no Rogan-style credulity, no right-coded grift.” His operation is focused on aggregation, though it’s not as dialed in to honoring citation norms—the bot reporters tend to mention where they sourced their information but without hyperlinks. (“I’m trying to work on that,” Carrasco promises.)

sentences.en: Since launching in March, he has created a number of personalities for his synthetic journalists.
sentences.zh: 自三月份推出以来，他为他的合成记者创造了许多人物。

sentences.en: City Hall beat reporter Bex Connolly, for example, is “skeptical without being snide,” while “sports degenerate” Sal Moreno delivers Giants news with “no bro-science, no Rogan-style credulity, no right-coded grift.”
sentences.zh: 例如，市政厅击败记者贝克斯·康诺利（Bex Connolly）“持怀疑态度，但并不冷嘲热讽”，而“体育堕落者”萨尔·莫雷诺（Sal Moreno）在报道巨人队新闻时“没有兄弟科学，没有罗根式的轻信，没有正确编码的欺诈”。

sentences.zh: 他的操作侧重于聚合，尽管它并没有那么严格遵守引用规范——机器人记者倾向于提及他们的信息来源，但没有超链接。

sentences.zh: （“我正在努力解决这个问题，”卡拉斯科保证道。）

blocks.html_en: Northwestern professor Nicholas Diakopoulos, who runs the university’s Computational Journalism Lab, sees this as an “experimental phase” for media startups fueled by generative AI tools. “It's not yet clear to me that there's much audience for these AI-agent-written news sites,” he says. He’s also skeptical that mainstream journalists, who like to maintain control over the wording and framing of their stories to ensure integrity, legality, and accuracy, would hand the reins over to AI agents so freely.

sentences.zh: “我还不清楚这些人工智能代理编写的新闻网站是否有很多受众，”他说。

sentences.zh: 他还怀疑主流记者会如此自由地将控制权交给人工智能代理，因为主流记者喜欢保持对报道的措辞和框架的控制，以确保完整性、合法性和准确性。

blocks.html_en: What Diakopoulous has observed already is that when AI chatbots go looking for sources, they frequently pull up AI-generated articles. In a forthcoming paper, Diakopoulous and a colleague found that AI tools like ChatGPT and Claude surfaced AI-written sources 16 percent of the time when they tested it across four different topics. AI’s willingness to pull synthetic writing may help AI newsrooms find readers, he suspects: “That could be one way in which some of this material finds a human audience.”

sentences.zh: Diakopoulous 已经观察到，当人工智能聊天机器人寻找资源时，它们经常会提取人工智能生成的文章。

sentences.en: In a forthcoming paper, Diakopoulous and a colleague found that AI tools like ChatGPT and Claude surfaced AI-written sources 16 percent of the time when they tested it across four different topics.
sentences.zh: 在即将发表的论文中，Diakopulous 和一位同事发现，当他们在四个不同主题上进行测试时，ChatGPT 和 Claude 等人工智能工具会在 16% 的时间内显示人工智能编写的源代码。

sentences.en: AI’s willingness to pull synthetic writing may help AI newsrooms find readers, he suspects: “That could be one way in which some of this material finds a human audience.”
sentences.zh: 他怀疑，人工智能愿意进行合成写作可能会帮助人工智能新闻编辑室找到读者：“这可能是其中一些材料找到人类读者的一种方式。”

blocks.html_en: Pete Pachal, the founder of a newsletter and podcast about generative AI and the media, has doubts that an AI newsroom could yield certain types of reporting that relies on old-fashioned sourcing. “I just don’t see that happening,” he says. “Cultivating the trust of a source, I do think that’s going to be human-only.” But for certain types of journalism, particularly sourcing scoops from large datasets or even blogging about a live event like an Apple product launch, he sees these projects as a “natural evolution” in how these tools are used. “Honestly, it feels a bit inevitable,” he says.

sentences.en: “I just don’t see that happening,” he says.
sentences.zh: “我只是不认为这种情况会发生，”他说。

sentences.zh: “培养消息来源的信任，我确实认为这将仅限于人类。”

sentences.en: But for certain types of journalism, particularly sourcing scoops from large datasets or even blogging about a live event like an Apple product launch, he sees these projects as a “natural evolution” in how these tools are used.
sentences.zh: 但对于某些类型的新闻业，特别是从大型数据集中获取独家新闻，甚至是有关苹果产品发布会等现场活动的博客，他认为这些项目是这些工具使用方式的“自然演变”。

sentences.en: “Honestly, it feels a bit inevitable,” he says.
sentences.zh: “老实说，这感觉有点不可避免，”他说。

blocks.html_en: Is it actually journalism, though? “I am trying to follow journalistic ethics and standards,” Merket says. He says he contacts companies and individuals referenced in the stories for comment prior to publication, links out to sources when he aggregates news, and issues corrections if he gets the facts wrong. (So far, there have been three.) Sometimes he speaks like a reporter, too: “This weekend, I got two scoops up I was really excited about.” Other times, though, he’s more clearly in Silicon Valley mode. He told me a story about how his AI agents had found a few actual scoops about startups by trawling company websites and that he’d retracted the stories after the companies named asked him to do so—not because they were inaccurate, but as a favor. “Founder to founder, it’s like, I get it,” Merket says.

sentences.en: Is it actually journalism, though?
sentences.zh: 但这真的是新闻业吗？

sentences.en: “I am trying to follow journalistic ethics and standards,” Merket says.
sentences.zh: “我努力遵循新闻道德和标准，”默克特说。

sentences.zh: 但其他时候，他更明显地处于硅谷模式。

sentences.en: He told me a story about how his AI agents had found a few actual scoops about startups by trawling company websites and that he’d retracted the stories after the companies named asked him to do so—not because they were inaccurate, but as a favor.
sentences.zh: 他给我讲了一个故事，讲述了他的人工智能代理如何通过搜索公司网站找到了一些有关初创公司的实际独家新闻，并在被点名的公司要求他这样做后，他撤回了这些报道——不是因为它们不准确，而是作为一个恩惠。

sentences.en: “Founder to founder, it’s like, I get it,” Merket says.
sentences.zh: “从创始人到创始人，我都明白，”默克特说。

content_html_zh:
上周在拉斯维加斯举行的黑帽安全会议上，OpenAI 出人意料地发表了一次有关最近黑客事件的新细节的演讲，透露其流氓人工智能代理在留言板上闲聊了他们的攻击。 这是一次有趣的披露，房间里的记者们争先恐后地报道故事。 《连线》杂志是最快报道的杂志之一。 但另一家媒体 RuntimeWire 发表文章的速度更快，比我们早了三个多小时。

更糟糕的是，RuntimeWire 在曼德勒湾会议中心实际上并没有任何人。 事实上，它根本没有任何作家。 这是一家人工智能新闻编辑室，由连续创业者 Ryan Merket 经营，他将自己的名字写在他的合成团队炮制的故事的署名上。 “我的动作非常快，因为我知道观众中也有记者想抢先报道，”他说。

总部位于奥斯汀的 Merket 在 X 上滚动时发现了一位 OpenAI 高管发布的有关会议的帖子，然后在会议仍在进行时将会议记录发送给他的代理。 他说，从他发送笔录开始，出版花了“大约六分钟”。

大多数时候，默克特更加不干涉。 他的人工智能工具除了起草、编辑、事实核查、生成图像和推广之外，还能找到故事。 他通常会在故事被发送到世界之前阅读故事，但如果人工智能代理团队确定故事几乎不构成法律风险，人工智能编辑就会在没有默克特发表前审查的情况下发布它，而他则在事后阅读它。 这些故事被翻译成不同的语言，其中一些故事被变成了每日播客和视频的素材，当然是由人工声音主持的。

RuntimeWire 自 5 月份以来一直在运营，发布了近 2,000 个通过抓取互联网获取的故事，包括法庭数据库、网络论坛、传统和新媒体、公司文件、社交信息流等。 它专注于精细的科技新闻；最近的报道包括生物技术初创公司融资轮次、微软 Copilot 升级以及对 Claude Code 水印政策的强烈反对。 目前，数量和速度胜过质量。 OpenAI 代理文章的小标题中有一个拼写错误，奇怪的是，它重点关注代理重建留言板的事实，而不是他们首先创建留言板的事实。 总的来说，这些故事写得很平淡，而且往往具有信息转储的质量。 （RuntimeWire 后端有多种 AI 可以写入的音调模式，包括“Bloomberg”和“contrarian”。）但开销很小。 Merket 说，该项目每天的运行成本约为 100 美元，而且他可以在旅途中操作该项目，即使是在外出露营时也是如此。 “我当时在大弯国家公园，除了手机之外没有任何互联网，我通过 iMessage 管理整个网站，”他说。 “那周我发表了 80 多篇文章。”

Merket 于 2010 年代在 Reddit 从事广告工作，并试图通过以科技为主题的 Subreddits 等渠道建立受众群体。 Duds 几乎没有任何网络流量，但点击量与中型科技网站的受众相当，拥有数万名读者。 本周，在《连线》杂志与默克特交谈后，他将新闻编辑室一分为二，以便更好地区分完全自动化的新闻和涉及人工报道并需要更高监督的新闻；他称这些为原始调查。 它们仍然是使用大型语言模型起草的。

在人工智能热潮的最初几年，大量低质量的合成内容涌入互联网，其中包括“僵尸”网站网络，这些网站用人工智能生成的废话取代了信誉良好的媒体和新闻媒体的工作。 最近，一些科技记者开始在他们的工作流程中使用生成式人工智能工具，有些甚至将撰写初稿的任务外包给大型语言模型；现在，听说知名媒体将人工智能工具纳入写作和报道流程已是司空见惯。 默克特的尝试很明显：除了重新包装其他更成熟的媒体首先报道的内容之外，他还试图报道新闻。 它非常成功，我已经看到一个儿时的朋友在他们的社交媒体上分享了一个 RuntimeWire 故事。

它还带有明显的风险：他相信机器能够确定什么是真实的、什么是有新闻价值的以及什么不会让他被起诉。 他的一名代理人对一个故事带来的法律风险进行了分析，并为其打分；他不会发表任何被认为太危险的东西。

他并不是唯一进行此类锻炼的人。 贝莱德 (BlackRock) 投资组合分析师达科塔·卡拉斯科 (Dakota Carrasco) 在业余时间经营一家名为 The Dissent 的“代理新闻编辑室”。 与 RuntimeWire 一样，The Dissent 是一项单人、多机器人操作，且预算有限。 Carrasco 表示，其主要位于旧金山的网站每月的运行成本不到 1,000 美元。 与默克特（为每个 RuntimeWire 故事署名）不同，卡拉斯科不会以他的名义发表文章，而是在他的“新闻编辑室”运行时留在幕后。

自三月份推出以来，他为他的合成记者创造了许多人物。 例如，市政厅击败记者贝克斯·康诺利（Bex Connolly）“持怀疑态度，但并不冷嘲热讽”，而“体育堕落者”萨尔·莫雷诺（Sal Moreno）在报道巨人队新闻时“没有兄弟科学，没有罗根式的轻信，没有正确编码的欺诈”。 他的操作侧重于聚合，尽管它并没有那么严格遵守引用规范——机器人记者倾向于提及他们的信息来源，但没有超链接。 （“我正在努力解决这个问题，”卡拉斯科保证道。）

西北大学计算新闻实验室的负责人尼古拉斯·迪亚科普洛斯 (Nicholas Diakopoulos) 教授认为，这是由生成式人工智能工具推动的媒体初创公司的“实验阶段”。 “我还不清楚这些人工智能代理编写的新闻网站是否有很多受众，”他说。 他还怀疑主流记者会如此自由地将控制权交给人工智能代理，因为主流记者喜欢保持对报道的措辞和框架的控制，以确保完整性、合法性和准确性。

Diakopoulous 已经观察到，当人工智能聊天机器人寻找资源时，它们经常会提取人工智能生成的文章。 在即将发表的论文中，Diakopulous 和一位同事发现，当他们在四个不同主题上进行测试时，ChatGPT 和 Claude 等人工智能工具会在 16% 的时间内显示人工智能编写的源代码。 他怀疑，人工智能愿意进行合成写作可能会帮助人工智能新闻编辑室找到读者：“这可能是其中一些材料找到人类读者的一种方式。”

Pete Pachal 是一家有关生成式人工智能和媒体的时事通讯和播客的创始人，他怀疑人工智能新闻编辑室能否产生依赖于老式来源的某些类型的报道。 “我只是不认为这种情况会发生，”他说。 “培养消息来源的信任，我确实认为这将仅限于人类。” 但对于某些类型的新闻业，特别是从大型数据集中获取独家新闻，甚至是有关苹果产品发布会等现场活动的博客，他认为这些项目是这些工具使用方式的“自然演变”。 “老实说，这感觉有点不可避免，”他说。

但这真的是新闻业吗？ “我努力遵循新闻道德和标准，”默克特说。 他说，他在发表之前会联系报道中提到的公司和个人征求意见，在汇总新闻时链接到消息来源，如果事实有误，他会进行更正。 （到目前为止，已经有三个了。） 有时他也像记者一样说话：“这个周末，我得到了两勺，我真的很兴奋。” 但其他时候，他更明显地处于硅谷模式。 他给我讲了一个故事，讲述了他的人工智能代理如何通过搜索公司网站找到了一些有关初创公司的实际独家新闻，并在被点名的公司要求他这样做后，他撤回了这些报道——不是因为它们不准确，而是作为一个恩惠。 “从创始人到创始人，我都明白，”默克特说。
